arc.summary: Wavy Life is SyWavy's water album. It starts in the spin of a breakup, drifts out into freedom and a new love by the shore, then turns to growing up, time spent away and coming back grown. The last song turns the boat around and points it home to St. Pete.

tracks.1: The breakup: caught spinning in circles, cut off, and still wishing her well.
tracks.2: Free of it now, and too proud to let her see him slip back.
tracks.3: Testing new water while the old phone signals go quiet.
tracks.4: A new love shows up from nowhere, clear as open water.
tracks.5: Riding the new thing loose, torn between staying put and drifting off.
tracks.6: Settled and calm for once, and drawn to someone new like a tide.
tracks.7: He names himself the Aqua Artist and stares out past the shore.
tracks.8: Looking back at every warning sign he drove right past.
tracks.9: A fantasy romance that ends with him asking where he stands.
tracks.10: Growing up, told as a baby learning to stand, walk and run.
tracks.11: Far from home and older for it, wondering what he missed.
tracks.12: The finale turns the boat around and heads home to St. Pete.

notes.body: The hook is gentle with her even as it admits he's caught. Every thought of the two of them drags him back into the same spin, and he still wants to fix things. It sets the album's first picture: water going around and around with nowhere to drain.
Core, crunch and working things out are all gym words. He talks about fixing the relationship the way he'd talk about training his abs.

notes.title: Whirlpool
notes.body: The appliance maker best known for its washers. Next to the window in the title, the heartbreak becomes the view through a washing machine's glass door, everything inside tumbling.

notes.title: Ride Along
notes.body: The 2014 cop comedy starring Ice Cube and Kevin Hart. The movie's title opens the line, and heart, which sounds like its star's last name, follows.

The breakup has moved to the phone. She has cut off contact, he wanted them to part on good terms and didn't get that, and now he's alone with it at home in St. Pete, where any small thing sets the spin going again.

notes.title: Offensive line
notes.body: In football, the offensive line exists to block. Here the term stands in for being blocked online by an ex.

notes.title: Tropicana Field
notes.body: The domed ballpark in St. Petersburg where the Tampa Bay Rays play, called the Trop by locals. Dome is also slang for your head, so he's stuck in his thoughts and stuck in his hometown at once.

notes.title: Carhartt
notes.body: The Detroit workwear brand whose canvas jeans and jackets became streetwear staples.
Snakes have no eyelids, so they really can't blink. He moves the old snake-in-the-grass saying onto the sand, where the two-faced stare without flinching.

notes.title: Bing
notes.body: Microsoft's search engine, the one almost nobody picks first. Looking there for how the story ends is a joke about having tried everything else.

notes.title: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
notes.body: The federal health agency whose guidelines everyone followed during the pandemic. He splits that word in two and offers to be the one who leads.

ref.name: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

notes.title: QVC
notes.body: The TV shopping channel lets buyers split a price into monthly payments, and its sister channel HSN, based in St. Pete, calls that FlexPay. Paying over time means not paying upfront, and upfront is also what she isn't with him.

The last verse is where the spin slows. He walks out and speaks his mind, and the cycle stops the way a Whirlpool washer does when the load is done. It's the first step toward the freedom of Triad, the next song.
It's the playground rhyme where love comes first, then marriage, then a baby in a baby carriage. She wants a carat for the wedding, and the baby after.

notes.title: Billy Butcher
notes.body: The British vigilante from The Boys who says oi and goes after superheroes.
The song opens in the cold: winter, an ex spreading stories, a frozen northern team. Against all that chill he's already gone, choosing a plane over a long walk.

notes.title: The Winter's Tale
notes.body: Shakespeare's late play about a king whose jealous accusations nearly destroy his family. Asking if she's Winter when she starts telling stories turns the title into a dig.

notes.title: Intel
notes.body: The computer chip maker. He wants the inside story, then makes clear he doesn't mean the processors.

notes.title: Denzel Washington
notes.body: He played an airline pilot in the 2012 film Flight. Choosing a plane over a hike puts him in the captain's seat.

notes.title: Latrell Sprewell
notes.body: The four-time All-Star guard also sold his own line of spinning rims, which is why his name follows a dizzy head. The fadeaway is a jump shot, and his last NBA team was Minnesota.

notes.title: Minnesota Timberwolves
notes.body: Minneapolis's NBA team, where Sprewell finished his career. Naming a team from the frozen north keeps the song's cold going.

notes.title: New Orleans Saints
notes.body: Saints fans in New Orleans chant Who Dat, short for asking who says they're going to beat the Saints. The line opens with that chant in his own words.

notes.title: Plankton
notes.body: The tiny villain from SpongeBob SquarePants, married to a computer named Karen, who turns up in the next line. Hoping the relationship holds up becomes a plank, the core exercise, hidden in his name.

notes.title: Barrett Firearms
notes.body: The Tennessee gun maker behind the best-known .50 caliber rifle. Cal also points west to California, and the brand lands as the punchline.

notes.title: Bugs Bunny
notes.body: The Looney Tunes rabbit hides in this line: bugging gives his name, and the carat she wants on her ring sounds like his carrot.
The chorus explains why there's no going back. He's doing well on his own, and pride is part of it: he won't let her catch him in the state he used to be in.

notes.title: Polo Ralph Lauren
notes.body: Ralph Lauren's shirt label, a staple for well-dressed guys in hip-hop for decades.

notes.title: Inside Out
notes.body: Pixar's 2015 film takes place inside a girl's head, and its lead character is an emotion named Joy. The line names the movie, then her.

notes.title: Ashton Kutcher
notes.body: He hosted Punk'd, the MTV prank show where celebrities got set up on camera. Don't be the one who gets fooled, he warns.

notes.title: Tonk
notes.body: A quick rummy card game that's a fixture at cookouts and card tables. Getting tonked means getting beaten, and dealing keeps the card game going in the same line.
Away from his phone and the drama, the verse turns inward. Silver jewelry and cologne are just him being himself, and the verse closes on Luther Vandross: the place he left was never a home.

notes.title: Chrome Hearts
notes.body: The Los Angeles luxury label known for silver jewelry and cross-and-heart designs. He breaks the name in two, with the heart on the label and the chrome on him.

notes.title: Luther Vandross
notes.body: The R&B singer's 1981 version of A House Is Not a Home is one of his best-loved recordings. The title says what he's learned about the place he left.

notes.title: Prince
notes.body: His 1984 hit When Doves Cry is the reference. Casting himself as Prince, he turns her tears into the song's doves.
Homegrown means he's from here, and it's also what you call weed grown at home, which fits a verse about smoking.

notes.title: Buzz Lightyear
notes.body: The space ranger from Toy Story, whose catchphrase is about flying to infinity and beyond. The line hides his full name along with that promise of forever, and a buzz is also the high from the smoking a few lines up.
The song opens on phone signals. Texts that used to go through now don't, he's reshuffled who gets his attention, and he's done giving credit to someone who gave little back.

notes.title: iMessage
notes.body: Apple's messaging app shows texts in blue bubbles. Green means the message went as a plain text, which usually happens when you've been blocked or the other phone is off.

notes.title: Jersey Shore
notes.body: MTV's 2009 reality show about roommates partying on the New Jersey coast. A shore and a jersey in one line put its name together.
Platonic slides into tectonic, the plates of rock that shift under the earth's surface. On a song named for how much of the planet is ocean, the way she moves shakes the ground.
The title is a fact: water covers about 71 percent of Earth's surface. On the water album, he borrows the number to size up love, which keeps the song tied to the sea.
Corduroy, the ribbed fabric, is often just called cord, which sounds like a chord on a guitar or piano. His pants and his songs share the word.

notes.title: Vladimir Putin
notes.body: Russia's president. Rushing sounds like Russian, so turning down Putin is his way of saying don't hurry him.
He knows his time away is hard on her, so he asks her to feel him there whenever he's back. The verse ends on a light coming on, the warmth he brings when he shows up.

notes.title: Terrell Owens
notes.body: The Hall of Fame receiver known as T.O., as famous for his touchdown celebrations as his catches. His name is the hype.

notes.title: Bol Bol
notes.body: The 7-foot-plus big man was playing for the Orlando Magic when this album came out. The pun is in his team's name.

notes.title: blink-182
notes.body: The pop-punk band behind All the Small Things (1999). A blinker in the line before sets up their name.

notes.title: Tina Fey
notes.body: She starred with Steve Carell in Date Night (2010), a comedy about a married couple's evening out gone wrong. The comparison promises an evening that's funny from start to finish.

notes.title: Keanu Reeves
notes.body: The actor known for all-black looks as John Wick and as Neo in The Matrix. His name breaks across two lines, with Reeves starting the second.

notes.title: Soft Cell
notes.body: The English synth-pop duo behind Tainted Love (1981). Calling his phone by their name sets up their biggest hit later in the same line.

notes.title: Taylor Swift
notes.body: A Swiftie is a Taylor Swift fan. That matters two lines later, when he admits who he grew up on.

notes.title: Kanye West
notes.body: Kanye cut into Taylor Swift's acceptance speech at the 2009 VMAs, starting one of pop's longest feuds. A Kanye kid falling for a Swiftie is why he wonders how they'd make it work.

The chorus is the album's turn. After the breakup songs, someone new arrives with no warning, and he's caught off guard by how sure he feels. The title also reads as the open sea, which keeps the water album on course.
No game and no rehearsed opener: the attraction ran both ways from the start, and her complexion never came into it. He likes her and says so.

notes.title: Big Ben
notes.body: The clock tower at the Houses of Parliament in London. Naming it is his way of saying he's watching the clock and wasting none of it.

notes.title: David Beckham
notes.body: The English soccer star, famous for free kicks that curled with spin. Said out loud, his name sounds like beckon, so after Big Ben the London theme rolls on and he calls her back.
The song opens torn. He liked what they had, hears from a friend that she's been with someone else, and still doesn't want her gone, all while he isn't exactly faithful himself.

notes.title: Mac Miller
notes.body: The Pittsburgh artist, who dated Ariana Grande from 2016 to 2018. The line pairs the two of them.

notes.title: Spider-Man
notes.body: Peter Parker's Aunt May dies in Spider-Man: No Way Home (2021), the loss that teaches him about responsibility. In Peter's place, he says, he'd have saved her.
Hang time is how long a player stays in the air on a jump. Here it's how long his dreads hang, and Kuy borrows the line on Intrusive Thoughts from Deep Voice Bastards.

notes.title: Harry Houdini
notes.body: The escape artist who could get out of anything. Pulling a Houdini means slipping away without a trace.

notes.title: Patrick Mahomes
notes.body: The Kansas City Chiefs quarterback, known for escaping pressure and throwing on the run. His team's city sets up the Kansas joke that follows.

notes.title: The Wizard of Oz
notes.body: In the 1939 film, Dorothy lands in Oz and realizes she isn't in Kansas anymore. He names himself its wizard, with rizz, slang for charm, swapped in.

notes.title: 0.5 selfie
notes.body: Phone cameras' 0.5x ultra-wide lens drove a 2022 trend of stretched, up-close photos. He plays the camera's zoom against drifting off.
The hook is the cruise in the title: easy, unhurried motion with someone he likes. He wants her to come along and keep it moving, no pressure.

notes.title: Frosted Flakes
notes.body: Tony the Tiger is the face of Kellogg's Frosted Flakes, so tiger leads right into flake, slang for bailing on someone. Bailing is what he says he won't do.
Here the easy mood breaks. He's been thinking hard about his own moves, and he can't understand how she could turn so cold.
Saying a guy is him is slang for being the one everyone talks about. He turns it into a pronoun joke: since he's him, other guys get a different pronoun.

notes.title: The Sims
notes.body: EA's life-simulation game, where players run the lives of digital people. He'd rather meet face to face than date someone who only exists on a screen.
Swiping is what you do with a card and what you do on a dating app. Right after saying he'd rather meet face to face, he admits he still does both.
The song opens settled: he's at peace, and love found him. She casts him as the pen, which makes her the ink, and pens click, so once they connect it's done.
A plug is slang for a connection, and it's also what goes into a wall socket, which is why the line ends with being wired in.

notes.title: The North Face
notes.body: The outdoor brand known for its puffer jackets. Asking her to warm him up like one makes her his coat.
The chorus turns ocean into a verb. Pulling her close works like the tide, and the title is the same idea at full size: moving a whole sea.

notes.title: Fergie
notes.body: The Black Eyed Peas singer whose 2005 hit My Humps comes back from the first verse. Her name also stands in for jiggy, as in Will Smith's Gettin' Jiggy wit It.

notes.title: Shakira
notes.body: Her 2006 hit Hips Don't Lie is the reference, set up by the line before it.
In basketball, a pick and roll often ends in an assist. He sets the pick, then passes to Cruise Jam, the song right before this one, whose hook is all about rolling.

notes.title: Paramore
notes.body: The Tennessee rock band, whose 2014 single Ain't It Fun won a Grammy. He borrows the title to ask why the dancing stopped, and the band's name sounds like paramour, an old word for a lover.

notes.title: Poland Spring
notes.body: The bottled water brand from Maine, at home on an album about water.

notes.title: The Omen
notes.body: Playboi Carti put out a song called The Omen in 2015, so fifteen is the year it came out.

notes.title: Toucan Sam
notes.body: The Froot Loops mascot with a rainbow beak. Fruity and a rainbow read as the pride flag, since she likes girls.

notes.title: Blazy Susan
notes.body: The pink rolling paper brand.

notes.title: Lindsay Lohan
notes.body: She starred in Freaky Friday (2003), where a mother and daughter wake up in each other's bodies. He borrows the title to ask for a wild end to the week.

notes.title: Wolverine
notes.body: Logan is Wolverine's real name and the title of his 2017 film. Put ex and man together and you get the X-Men, the team he's best known for.

notes.title: 50 Cent
notes.body: His 2003 song Many Men (Wish Death) is about outlasting the people who wanted him gone. He says he was born facing that kind of opposition.

notes.title: Wheezy
notes.body: The squeaky toy penguin from Toy Story 2, named for the wheeze his broken squeaker makes.
He gives himself the album's title role here: the Aqua Artist, standing at the edge and staring as far out as he can see. The verse is about patience, trusting that what he's after is out there.

notes.title: Marlin
notes.body: The clownfish father in Finding Nemo, who crosses the ocean to find his son. The search pays off in the end, and that's the promise here.

notes.title: Target
notes.body: The retailer's logo is a red bullseye. Sharing a location that lands dead center is the pun.
A loose kite drifts up and away, and high as a kite is the old saying for being stoned. The next line makes clear which kind of high he means.
The bridge rests on one irony. She praises the way he talks, yet hasn't noticed the two of them stopped talking. He says it again and again until the silence is the loudest thing in the song.

notes.title: Kelly Rowland
notes.body: A member of Destiny's Child with Beyoncé and Michelle Williams. Her last name sounds like rolling, and the next lines work the group's name in too.
The outro is the album's softest moment. He admits he was wrong and that the parting came without a farewell. What steadies him is that everyone lives in the same world, held by the same water.
Being in la la land means daydreaming. She isn't paying attention.

notes.title: Walter White
notes.body: The chemistry teacher at the center of Breaking Bad, who goes by Walt. His name keeps the rhyme going between the Star Wars queen before it and the Warriors forward after it.

notes.title: Magic Conch
notes.body: The toy shell in SpongeBob SquarePants that answers whatever you ask it. That's where he goes for advice.

notes.title: Ariel
notes.body: The mermaid from Disney's The Little Mermaid. Calling her his Ariel keeps the album's water theme going.

notes.title: Robin Thicke
notes.body: His 2013 hit Blurred Lines is the reference, set up by blurry signs that keep the song's road-sign theme going.

The first verse is set at the gym. He counts down a lift and splits one piece of equipment across two lines so its second half rhymes with how she makes him feel. Being around her has become a workout, and he wants his guard back up.
The chorus is the confession: the warnings were there from the start, and he ignored them. Every reference that follows is another sign he passed.

notes.title: Padmé Amidala
notes.body: The queen and senator from the Star Wars prequels, who dies of a broken heart in Revenge of the Sith. That's why her name fits something that's killing him.

notes.title: Andre Iguodala
notes.body: The forward won four titles with the Golden State Warriors. He calls himself a warrior and finishes the line with Iguodala's name.

notes.title: Tua Tagovailoa
notes.body: The Miami Dolphins quarterback. His first name sounds like to ya, so a pass that can't reach her lands on a Florida quarterback.

notes.title: Hooters
notes.body: The restaurant chain, founded in Clearwater in 1983. He twists the saying about there being no I in team, then points to the two O's in its name.

notes.title: Austin Powers
notes.body: Mike Myers' swinging '60s spy from the late-'90s comedies, who calls everyone baby. The compliment is pure Austin.

notes.title: Gwen Stacy
notes.body: Peter Parker's girlfriend, whose deadly fall is one of Spider-Man's best-known stories. He says he never lets anything drop, the opposite of what happened to her.

notes.title: Jenna Ortega
notes.body: The actor whose Netflix series Wednesday was a breakout hit in late 2022. Her name stands for the kind of woman he wants.

notes.title: Thon Maker
notes.body: The seven-foot center the Milwaukee Bucks drafted in 2016. Rising to his height is how far up he's going.

notes.title: Vita Vea
notes.body: The Tampa Bay Buccaneers' huge defensive tackle, listed around 350 pounds. Buck points to the Bucs and fifty is his jersey number, right after a center the Milwaukee Bucks drafted.

notes.title: Keurig K-Cups
notes.body: Keurig's single-serve coffee pods. A few lines after nodding off, he's propping himself up with two stimulants at once.
In Roman numerals, V stands for five, so the letter and the number are the same thing.
The song ends unscripted. He wonders out loud whether it was caution at all, admits he lets things slide, and shrugs, which proves the point of the song.
Telly is slang for a hotel, and the first verse is a night at one, paid for so they can stay.
The second verse is pure daydream: a rocket, a fairy tale, a video game. She's the clear sky after the clouds, and every image has him rising.

notes.title: Tinker Bell
notes.body: The fairy from Peter Pan. Pairing a bell with Tink spells out her full name, and a fairy tale follows in the next line.

notes.title: Final Fantasy
notes.body: Square Enix's long-running role-playing series. His last fantasy and the game's name are the same words, and the cloud his head was in is also Cloud, the hero of Final Fantasy VII.

notes.title: Victoria's Secret PINK
notes.body: PINK is Victoria's Secret's label for younger shoppers. With secrets earlier in the line, pink means the brand and something more private.

notes.title: The Deep
notes.body: A sea-powered superhero in Amazon's The Boys, a send-up of Aquaman. Hanging with his own crew, he makes clear they aren't the show's.

notes.title: Nelly
notes.body: His 2002 summer hit Hot in Herre is the source. Instead of taking clothes off, he heads for the sink, since water is this album's answer to everything.

notes.title: Jay-Z
notes.body: His 2004 single Dirt Off Your Shoulder made brushing off your shoulder the gesture for shrugging off haters. When he does it, a wave is what he sees.
The chorus flips the fantasy. He spent days hoping she'd keep her distance, because both of them know what happens when she doesn't.
The last verse is all questions: why she'd trade him in, why she moves the way she does, whether she loves him. The OutKast lines bring a joke, but the ending is a plain ask.

notes.title: OutKast
notes.body: André 3000 of OutKast goes by Three Stacks, so counting stacks up to three lands on the duo. Their 1996 single Elevators (Me & You) is behind the elevator and escalator lines that follow.
The hook is a body falling and getting back up. Her love knocked him to the floor, and the song is him working his way to his feet.
Here her words land like bullets, each thought another wound, and he can't see how she came through untouched. By the end of the verse he's back up.

notes.title: Kevlar
notes.body: The DuPont fiber used in bulletproof vests. A mind made of it can take a hit, and that's the toughness he's had to grow.

notes.title: Miami
notes.body: 305 is Miami's area code, the number Pitbull built his Mr. 305 name on. With the sea in the same line, it puts the night on a Miami beach.
The bridge widens from one breakup to growing up: a baby learning to walk, then run, a child turning into a man. It's where Wavy Life turns from love to getting older.

notes.title: Andrew Schulz
notes.body: The comedian whose podcast was first called Flagrant 2. Being flagrant too says the show's old name out loud, and the odd spelling is his last name.
Scotti is a weed strain, so he's asking if she wants to smoke. The same strain came up on Why Me?, in ? (Cry).
A hot tamale is a cinnamon candy and slang for a good-looking woman, and the heat is going up.
The title is Disney's Fantasia, the 1940 film set to classical music.

notes.title: VLONE
notes.body: The streetwear label from A$AP Bari of A$AP Mob. Its name is one letter off from alone, which is the joke when a homesick kid wears it.
The opening is homesickness. He's been fending for himself for a long stretch, and it's worst late at night when sleep won't come. This is the album's time away.

notes.title: La Di Da Di
notes.body: The 1985 record by Doug E. Fresh and Slick Rick. Doug E. Fresh was known as the Human Beatbox, which is why it follows beatboxing.

notes.title: Tutankhamun
notes.body: The Egyptian boy king whose tomb, found in 1922, was full of gold, including his famous mask. He's looking at gold the way the people who opened it did.
The chorus is the album's growing-up line. Leaving made him older and wiser, and the question he keeps asking is what changed while he was gone.

notes.title: BlueChew
notes.body: BlueChew sells chewable pills for erections online. True blue means loyal, but adding chew turns it into the brand, and the next line says what it's for.
He stops to tell his mother he loves her, then pushes back on anyone who thinks he's been idle. He's been focused on his own path while they wasted time.

notes.title: King Bach
notes.body: Andrew Bachelor, the comedian who was the most-followed star on Vine, where every video ran six seconds. That's how long she gets before he texts.

notes.title: The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker
notes.body: Nintendo's GameCube Zelda, set on a flooded world where Link sails between islands and uses a baton to steer the wind. It's a fitting finale for a water album.

ref.name: The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker

notes.title: Polaroid
notes.body: The instant camera. Shaking the photo to develop it was made famous by OutKast's Hey Ya!, though Polaroid itself said not to.

notes.title: Chrollo Lucilfer
notes.body: The calm, sharp-dressed leader of the Phantom Troupe in Hunter x Hunter. He borrows the character's cool.

notes.title: Call of Duty
notes.body: Danger Close is a perk in Call of Duty: Black Ops 2 that makes explosives hit harder. He's the big threat with the upgrade on.

notes.title: Dirk Nowitzki
notes.body: The Dallas Mavericks star who wore 41 and made the one-legged fadeaway his signature. The fadeaway and his name come first, then the number.
This is the homecoming the album has been building to. He turns around, asks what's changed, and heads back to St. Pete sure that he's coming back with something to show for it.

notes.title: St. Petersburg
notes.body: SyWavy's hometown, called the Burg by locals. Heading back there is where Wavy Life ends up.

notes.title: Microsoft Office
notes.body: Points that have power make PowerPoint, and his word makes Word: two Microsoft Office programs in one line.
The chorus plays on wake three ways: the wind from the game, the trail a boat leaves, and opening your eyes. He wakes to still air and nothing to regret.
She's from overseas, so studying a broad is also study abroad, the semester spent in another country.

notes.title: Darth Vader
notes.body: The Star Wars villain who reveals he is Luke Skywalker's father. The line asks about Skywalker's father and tucks the answer into a word about invading.
Salsa is a dance and a sauce, and the next line turns it into a saucer. With an abduction in the same line, it's a flying saucer carrying off what they had.

notes.title: Nicaragua
notes.body: The Central American country where the CIA backed rebels against the government in the 1980s. It caps a run of Spanish in the verse.
Wavy Life doesn't close with a bow: the music keeps moving and the change isn't finished. A sound is also a wide inlet of the sea, so on the water album the music ends as open water.
